name: Reaction system

card.summary: A looksmax.org forum framework for how posts earn reactions, covering visibility, humor, timing and user status, used to gain community standing and engagement.
card.note: Forum-specific folk theory; it describes one community's habits rather than a general social principle.

quick.overview:
The reaction system is the name used on looksmax.org for the way posts collect reactions (reps) from other members. Two long member-written guides lay out what they believe drives those reactions: how many users see a post, the type of content, the age and status of the poster, and thread timing.

The looks-related payoff is indirect: more reactions mean more visibility and standing in the community where people get feedback on their faces, routines and progress, and the guides treat reading the room as a skill.
quick.how: According to the guides, members raise a post's reach by placing it early in an active thread, avoiding dead threads, and using formatting such as bold or larger text. They describe short jokes as reacting better than long informational posts, and advise on thread topics with high potential for engagement.
quick.risks: No physical risks. Reaction counts are a community metric, and the guides themselves note that status on the site strongly shapes the response, so results vary by poster.

lead: The reaction system is a framework discussed on looksmax.org for understanding how posts gain reactions, the small votes members give each other. The best-known write-ups are a 'Complete Guide to the Reaction System' and a follow-up for advanced users [1][2].

The guides argue that reactions follow visibility: every user has some chance of reacting to a post, so more users seeing it means more reactions. They list factors such as font size and bold text, placement on early pages of a thread, whether a thread is still active, the type of content, and the poster's age and status on the forum [1]. The advanced guide covers thread life cycles, topics with high engagement potential and unwritten site rules [2].

chain: Understand what makes posts visible and well received
Post in ways that attract reactions
More visibility and standing in the forum where looks feedback is exchanged
angle.text: The guides frame reactions as a skill members can optimise. A higher profile in a looks-focused community means more attention for the photos, questions and progress posts that members share.

infobox: Visibility, humor, thread timing, user status

paras: The basic guide divides the question into what determines how much reaction a post receives. It says reach is the starting point and lists ways to affect it: larger or bold text, avoiding threads that have gone dead, and posting early in a thread rather than on its fiftieth page [1].

It also argues that jokes tend to collect more reactions than useful information, for two reasons: they are shorter, so more users read them, and they leave a stronger emotional impression. A further section discusses an 'old user bias', in which long-standing members receive reactions for comments that would draw few from newcomers [1].

The second guide, aimed at experienced users, describes the life span of a thread as depending on its potential for engagement. It names controversial subjects and threads about the community itself as high-engagement, and very short or very long threads as low-engagement because they give readers little to respond to or too much [2].

It also covers the life cycle of a thread, cautions about revival of old threads under forum rules, and a set of 'shadow rules', unspoken norms of the site. Replies under the guide include members who say status on the site matters more than the content of a post [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the reaction system is treated as a practical craft for getting noticed, and the two guides are the main reference [1][2].

claims.claim: Posts get reactions in proportion to how many users see them
claims.believers: The guide's author says every user has a chance of reacting, so formatting, placement on early pages and avoiding dead threads raise reach [1].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this forum's reaction counts.
